coverage.label: Monday 31 August 2026, 0700 SGT → Tuesday 1 September 2026, 0700 SGT

global.headline: IRAN FIRES ON US BASES IN JORDAN AND THE UAE AFTER THE LARAK STRIKE; TRUMP VOWS TO 'HIT IRAN HARD'
summary: The month-long military lull has now broken in both directions. After US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps mounted a combined missile-and-drone operation it named "Punishment of the Aggressor," hitting the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan — both of which host US forces. Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles shortly after the IRGC announced the attack. Iran also claimed to have struck US military targets in the United Arab Emirates; the UAE air force said it responded to a drone detected over its territorial waters approaching from Iran, but denied that Al Minhad air base itself was hit. No US casualties were reported from either country. Iranian state broadcasters said the Larak strike killed or wounded both IRGC personnel and civilians; no independently verified figure has emerged.

President Trump told Fox News on Monday that the US would hit Iran hard in return for Tehran targeting American forces, and posted an AI-generated video to Truth Social appearing to depict the bombing of Kharg Island — the terminal that handles the bulk of Iran's crude exports, floated as a target since July and still never struck. US officials indicated the Larak launchers may have been preparing a previously unseen type of Iranian naval mine, a claim that sits directly against Trump's own 28 August declaration that the Strait of Hormuz was clear of mines and his "MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026" post. Brent crude rose 2.93% on Monday to US$90.69 a barrel, back above US$90 for the first time since the strike pause began; between 6 and 8 million barrels a day are still moving through the strait.

The exchange lands on an Iranian economy in visible collapse. The rial hit 2 million to the US dollar on 23 August, a roughly 47-fold devaluation in two years; inflation was 87.9% in data released in late July, unemployment reached 9.1% in the spring, and GDP is forecast to contract 5.4% this year. Central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in August that Iran is essentially no longer exporting oil. Washington's Operation Economic Outcast sanctions campaign, which reached a UAE branch of Egypt's Banque Misr last week, continues in parallel — the military and financial tracks now running at once rather than one substituting for the other.
global.geopolitical: Two things changed on Monday that a month of sanctions had not. First, Iran demonstrated it will still answer a kinetic strike with a kinetic strike across borders, pulling Jordan and the UAE back into a war they have spent weeks trying to exit — the UAE having already suspended all trade with Iran on 20 August after a similar missile incident, leaving it with little economic leverage left to escalate. Second, Washington's stated justification, that Iran was preparing fresh mines for Hormuz, undercuts its own claim to have cleared and secured the strait, and hands Tehran the argument that the US declaration of success was premature. The Kharg Island video is the sharpest signal yet that the administration is willing to threaten Iran's export lifeline directly, a step it has held back from through five months of strikes; carrying it out would convert a blockade into the destruction of the asset itself.
global.socioeconomic: Brent's move back above US$90 shows how thin the market's confidence in the reopening story always was: three days of optimism on demining claims were erased by one night of exchanged fire. For Iranians the arithmetic is harsher still — an 87.9% inflation rate and a currency at 2 million to the dollar mean the war is now felt mainly at the shop counter and the petrol pump rather than in the air, with the fuel shortfall reported last week still unresolved. For shipping, the mine claim matters more than the missiles: war-risk premiums and the decision to use the Omani rather than the Iranian corridor turn on whether the waterway is actually safe, and Monday's events argue that nobody, including Washington, currently knows.

global.headline: NEPAL FLOOD DEATHS PASS 900 AS THE MISSING NEARLY DOUBLE TO OVER 4,200; KATHMANDU PUTS RECOVERY AT S$6.4 BILLION AND ASKS THE UN CLIMATE FUND TO PAY
summary: The toll from last week's Himalayan flash floods rose to 903 dead in Nepal on Monday, while the number listed as missing nearly doubled to 4,247 — including 592 foreign nationals — as authorities reconciled village-level registers along the 72km stretch of the Trishuli river hit when part of a glacier collapsed near the China border on 26 August. The jump is a bookkeeping revision, not a second disaster, but it makes this the deadliest single event in Nepal's modern record and leaves the final figure genuinely unknown.

Rescue work has narrowed to the hydropower tunnels. Of the 933 hydropower workers unaccounted for, the government says more than 100 may still be alive inside tunnels at the Trishuli 3A and 3B projects, where army teams broke through late Saturday and began pumping oxygen to those trapped. The army has pulled 254 people out of the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 project and 18 from the 20MW Langtang Khola scheme. Indian and Chinese tunnelling teams are on site or en route.

Nepal's government put the cost of recovery at about S$6.4 billion (US$5 billion) and asked the UN's special fund for climate-disaster recovery to help meet it. Maheshwar Dhakal, climate change chief at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, said human-caused warming was a factor in the glacial collapse and framed the claim in terms of inequity: "Those who have contributed the least are suffering the most." Natural disasters have cost Nepal close to US$7 billion cumulatively over the past four decades — meaning this single week is being priced at roughly three-quarters of everything that came before it.
global.geopolitical: Nepal is turning a disaster into a test case for the loss-and-damage machinery that rich countries agreed to in principle and have funded thinly in practice. A formal, costed request tied to an attributable glacial collapse is exactly the kind of claim the fund was designed for and has never had to answer at this scale; how it responds will shape whether other Himalayan and small-island states bring similar bills. The presence of Indian and Chinese rescue teams in the same tunnels, on a border where both powers compete for influence, is its own quiet contest — and China's handling of the Tibet side, where campaigners accuse Beijing of concealing the scale of losses, keeps the two halves of one disaster on very different information footings.
global.socioeconomic: A US$5 billion recovery bill is enormous against a Nepali economy of roughly US$44 billion, and the composition of the damage compounds it: the hydropower sector that was meant to be Nepal's export earner is precisely what the flood destroyed, along with the workforce operating it. Rebuilding means either heavy external borrowing on top of existing debt, or a reconstruction financed by the climate fund — which is why the attribution argument is not rhetorical for Kathmandu but fiscal. With 4,247 people still missing and mass burials under way, the household-level economics arrive first: families cannot settle estates, claim insurance, or remarry without death certificates that a missing-persons list does not produce.

global.headline: XI, PUTIN AND MODI CONVENE IN BISHKEK FOR THE SCO'S 25TH-ANNIVERSARY SUMMIT, WITH IRAN AND TURKEY AT THE TABLE
summary: The 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit opened in Bishkek on Monday under Kyrgyz chairmanship, running two days and marking 25 years since the bloc's founding, under the motto "Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity." Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Narendra Modi, Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian are attending the plenary chaired by President Sadyr Japarov; Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan is present as a dialogue partner rather than a member.

The declared agenda is regional security, terrorism and transnational threats, trade, energy, transport connectivity and digital cooperation, with the wars in West Asia and Ukraine expected to feature in the discussions rather than the communique. The bilaterals are the substance: Putin is scheduled to meet Xi and, separately, Pezeshkian; Modi is meeting Putin on the India-Russia strategic partnership, including energy and defence, and Japarov on the sidelines.

The gathering is being read — including by the New York Times, which framed it as a display of the leverage two wars have handed Xi — less as a functioning alliance than as a photograph China wants taken: the leaders of Russia, India and Iran in one room while Washington runs simultaneous pressure campaigns against two of them. No binding security commitment is on the table, and the members' own disputes (India-Pakistan, India-China border) remain unresolved.
global.geopolitical: The SCO's value to Beijing has always been symbolic rather than operational, and symbolism is worth more this year than usual. Two of the leaders in the room are the direct targets of American sanctions campaigns, and a third, Modi, has been pushed toward hedging by US tariff pressure — which lets Xi present the bloc as the assembly point for states declining to take Washington's side without asking any of them to actually commit to anything. The limits are equally visible: the SCO has no mutual-defence clause, its two largest Asian members dispute their own border, and Turkey attends while remaining in NATO. What the summit reliably produces is optionality for its members in bilateral negotiations with the US, and that is the point.
global.socioeconomic: The concrete agenda items — transport connectivity, energy and payments — are where the bloc has real if slow effects: overland corridors and non-dollar settlement arrangements that matter most to precisely the members that have been cut out of dollar clearing. For India, the Putin bilateral on energy and defence is a live commercial question about discounted Russian crude and existing weapons dependencies, not a gesture. For Central Asian hosts like Kyrgyzstan, the summit is an infrastructure-financing venue first and a security forum second.

global.headline: US ARMY SECRETARY DAN DRISCOLL RESIGNS AFTER CLASHING WITH HEGSETH OVER A STRIPPED PROMOTIONS LIST
summary: Dan Driscoll, the Army's civilian secretary since February 2025, submitted his resignation on Monday effective 3 September, on short notice and after months of friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The White House confirmed the departure and issued a statement praising his service.

Reporting on the rupture centres on a promotions dispute: Hegseth is said to have removed four officers — two Black men and two women — from a promotions list after Driscoll declined to do so himself. Driscoll's friendship with Vice-President JD Vance had given him some protection inside a Pentagon where Hegseth had not warmed to him.

The exit is the latest in a run of senior departures from the Department of Defense under Hegseth, and it comes with the Army carrying the largest share of an Iran campaign now in its seventh month, with 18 US personnel killed and more than 757 wounded on the Pentagon's own count.
global.geopolitical: A service secretary leaving over who gets promoted, rather than over strategy or budget, is a signal about how the Pentagon's civilian control is currently working: the dispute was about the Defense Secretary reaching into a service's own personnel process, and the service secretary lost. Allies and adversaries read continuity at the top of the US military establishment as a proxy for the reliability of American commitments, and this is a further data point in an unusually high turnover cycle during an active war. That Driscoll's protection ran through a personal relationship with the Vice-President rather than through his office says something about where authority actually sits.
global.socioeconomic: The Army is mid-campaign and mid-recruiting cycle, and a promotions list stripped along apparent race and sex lines is precisely the kind of episode that reaches serving officers faster than any policy document. The practical costs are retention and the signal sent to mid-career officers about whether merit boards will hold; the institutional cost is a leaderless service department at a moment when the Army is absorbing casualties, sustaining a naval blockade's ground support, and competing for a war supplement inside a defence budget Congress has still not passed.

global.headline: US SUPREME COURT LETS TRUMP KEEP BUILDING THE WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM, 5-4, ON STANDING GROUNDS
summary: The Supreme Court on Monday granted the Trump administration's emergency application and lifted lower-court orders that had halted above-ground work on the new White House ballroom, allowing construction to continue indefinitely. The vote was 5-4, and the ruling was unsigned.

The court's stated basis was narrow: the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the challenge, likely lacks standing to sue. That leaves the underlying question — whether a president may demolish and redesign parts of the White House without congressional approval — formally undecided. A district judge had ruled in March that construction must stop unless Congress signed off.

The National Trust said the majority "did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal," and that the decision does not resolve its central argument that each president is "a temporary steward of the People's House."
global.geopolitical: Domestic, but with a familiar shape: an emergency-docket order that hands the executive a practical win while declining to rule on the executive's authority. Standing doctrine has become the mechanism by which the merits of separation-of-powers disputes are deferred, and deferral favours whoever already holds the bulldozer — by the time the question is justiciable, the building is built. That pattern, repeated across this term's emergency applications, is itself the consequential fact rather than the ballroom.
global.socioeconomic: The direct costs are borne privately — the project is donor-funded — but the precedent is not. If the only parties with a plausible interest in preserving a federally owned landmark are held to lack standing, the practical enforcement of historic-preservation law over executive-branch property narrows to whatever Congress chooses to legislate and fund. For the preservation sector, which litigates almost entirely through organisations like the National Trust, a standing ruling of this kind is more restrictive than any single construction permit.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE WEIGHS DAILY SOCIAL MEDIA TIME LIMITS FOR TEENS AND WILL MANDATE AGE ASSURANCE, WITH LAWS DUE IN EARLY 2027
summary: Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo has set out a package of mandatory safeguards the government is considering for users under 18, with a daily time limit on social media among them. The target is the design features that drive compulsive use — autoplay, infinite scroll and algorithmic feeds — with Teo describing a time limit as a way of creating a natural stopping point. No specific limit has been set.

Age assurance of 13 will be made mandatory on social media platforms, and platforms that cannot or will not implement the stronger under-18 protections could instead be required to raise their minimum access age to 18 outright. Six services already designated under Singapore's online safety code — Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and HardwareZone — would be first. The approach mirrors the one already applied to app stores: operators propose their own age-estimation, inference or verification methods, and the regulator assesses whether they are robust enough.
Legislative changes are expected to be tabled in early 2027. The measures sit alongside MDDI's Screen Smart from the Start movement, launched in May 2026, and its Be Screen Smart portal for parents.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is positioning between the two live models: Australia's outright under-16 ban and the EU/UK duty-of-care approach that regulates design rather than access. Choosing to mandate age assurance while holding the minimum-age increase in reserve as a penalty for non-compliance is a distinctly Singaporean structure — it puts the burden of proof on the platforms and keeps the harsher option as leverage. If it works, it gives other jurisdictions a template that does not require the political cost of a ban; if the platforms stall, Singapore has pre-committed to the ban anyway.
singapore.socioeconomic: A hard time limit would be the first design-level intervention here to touch the core engagement mechanics of the six largest platforms, and the compliance cost falls on them rather than on schools or parents. For households, the practical shift is from parental discretion to a default set by regulation — which changes the argument at home from whether to limit to how to work within the limit. The risks are the familiar ones: age assurance means more identity data collected about minors, and teenagers route around blunt limits, so the enforcement design will matter more than the announced number.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE DEPLOYS A POLICE DISASTER VICTIM IDENTIFICATION TEAM AND AIRLIFTS SUPPLIES TO NEPAL
summary: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Monday that Singapore will deploy a specialist Singapore Police Force team of Disaster Victim Identification officers to Nepal, at the Nepali government's request, along with humanitarian supplies drawn from both civilian stocks and the Singapore Armed Forces.

The package was conveyed by Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan in a phone call with his Nepali counterpart Shisir Khanal. It comes on top of the government's US$100,000 (about S$127,000) contribution on 28 August to the Singapore Red Cross public appeal, which hit its S$1 million target within three days.

MFA's Crisis Response Team has been on the ground in Nepal since 27 August providing consular support. Nine Singaporeans remain unaccounted for. Separately, local charity RLAF pledged S$50,000 and opened its own appeal, and MPs Dinesh Vasu Dash and Alex Yam publicly urged compassion after online comments questioned the nationality of the missing Singaporeans.
singapore.geopolitical: DVI officers are a specific and unglamorous kind of aid: with 903 confirmed dead and 4,247 missing, Nepal's constraint is no longer rescue capacity but the forensic identification of remains, and Singapore is supplying the scarce skill rather than the visible airlift. It is the same niche-capability diplomacy Singapore has used after the Boxing Day tsunami and MH370 — low-cost, high-credibility, and specifically requested rather than offered. Sending police alongside SAF stocks also keeps the deployment civilian-led, which matters for a mission on a Nepal-China border where two larger neighbours are already operating.
singapore.socioeconomic: For the families of the nine missing Singaporeans, DVI capability is the difference between an indefinite wait and a legal death — identification is what unlocks estates, insurance and closure. The public dimension is less comfortable: the MPs' intervention responded to comments questioning whether naturalised Singaporeans among the missing counted as "our own," a reminder that the citizenship-and-belonging argument surfaces fastest when a crisis puts names and origins in the news.

singapore.headline: TOMMY KOH WINS THE 2026 RAMON MAGSAYSAY AWARD, THE FOURTH SINGAPOREAN TO DO SO
summary: Veteran diplomat Tommy Koh was named a 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardee on Monday, cited for a six-decade career as diplomat, negotiator and teacher, and for work bringing states with competing interests toward common ground. He is honoured alongside Bangladeshi humanitarian Runa Khan and Myanmar activist Bo Kyi.

The citation rests substantially on international law: Koh presided over the Third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea and was central to concluding the negotiations that produced UNCLOS in 1982 — the treaty that still governs maritime claims from the South China Sea to the Arctic.
Koh is the fourth Singaporean recipient, after Lim Kim San (1965), Goh Keng Swee (1972) and Willing Hearts founder Tony Tay (2017). The 68th awards ceremony is on 15 November 2026.
singapore.geopolitical: The award lands at a moment when the instrument Koh is being honoured for is under visible strain: UNCLOS is the legal frame for the South China Sea disputes that Southeast Asia cannot resolve, and for a Strait of Hormuz where transit passage has been suspended by force for six months. Recognising the architect of a consensus treaty is, implicitly, a statement about what the region thinks it is losing. For Singapore specifically, Koh's career is the template of the small-state strategy — influence through legal craft and convening rather than weight — which is why the honour reads here as institutional as much as personal.
singapore.socioeconomic: UNCLOS is not an abstraction for a country whose economy rests on the freedom of the sea lanes: the exclusive economic zone regime, the transit-passage rules and the dispute mechanisms Koh helped negotiate are the legal basis on which Singapore's port and its shipping registry operate. The award also arrives as Singapore leans on soft-power assets — legal expertise, arbitration, convening capacity — as a growth sector in their own right, not merely as diplomacy.

singapore.headline: MINLAW IMPOSES A THREE-DAY COOLING-OFF PERIOD ON ALL UNSECURED LICENSED MONEYLENDER LOANS FROM 15 SEPTEMBER
summary: The Ministry of Law announced on Monday that from 15 September, every unsecured loan from a licensed moneylender will carry a mandatory cooling-off period of three business days, during which a borrower may cancel.

If a borrower cancels, no interest may be charged and the total repayable cannot exceed the principal. Moneylenders may retain only a capped share of the loan approval fee: a maximum of S$50 on loans of S$5,000 or less, and a maximum of 3.5% of principal (not exceeding the approval fee) on larger loans.
MinLaw framed the design as balancing a borrower's chance to reconsider against compensating lenders for work already done in granting the loan.
singapore.geopolitical: Not a foreign-policy matter, but part of a consumer-credit regime that Singapore exports by example across the region, where licensed moneylending sits alongside a much larger unlicensed market. The regulatory bet is that friction in the licensed channel does not push borrowers into the unlicensed one — the standard failure mode of moneylending reform elsewhere, and the thing enforcement data will need to show over the next year.
singapore.socioeconomic: Three business days is aimed squarely at the impulse loan taken under pressure, and the fee caps mean cancellation is close to costless — a S$50 ceiling on small loans removes the penalty that would otherwise make the right to cancel theoretical. Against a backdrop of retrenchments at their highest since 2023 and rising cost pressure, the measure targets the point in a household's finances where a short-term loan turns into a debt spiral. The counter-risk remains loan sharks: if licensed lenders tighten approvals in response to the cancellation risk, marginal borrowers move to the channel with no cooling-off period at all.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE OPENS A S$300 MILLION GRANT FOR EARLY-STAGE TECHNOLOGIES AS RIE2025 CLOSES WITH BUSINESS R&D UP 64%
summary: A new S$300 million grant under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan will fund nascent technologies through the gap between laboratory result and commercial viability — sustaining promising work until it can be licensed out or spun into a company.

It is the first substantive instrument announced under RIE2030, the record S$37 billion five-year commitment (about 1% of GDP) unveiled by Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong in December 2025 and running from April 2026.

The accompanying RIE2025 report closed the previous cycle with S$28 billion in public R&D funding disbursed, a 64% rise in business R&D spending, growth in the medtech sector, and a stated intent to deepen public-private co-funding under the new plan.
singapore.geopolitical: R&D intensity at 1% of GDP in public funding alone is a deliberate positioning against a region where research capacity is concentrating in China, and against export controls that make technological self-sufficiency a security question rather than an economic one. The specific choice to fund the valley of death between lab and market — rather than more basic research — says Singapore judges its weakness to be translation, not discovery. That is also the segment most exposed to a global venture funding environment that has not recovered.
singapore.socioeconomic: A 64% rise in business R&D spending is the more meaningful number in the RIE2025 report than the S$28 billion of public money, because it is the private co-investment that determines whether public research produces domestic jobs rather than papers. The S$300m grant is small relative to the S$37 billion plan, but it is aimed at the stage where most publicly funded discoveries die — and in an economy under retrenchment pressure with a services outlook still negative, the case for the whole programme rests on whether spin-offs and licensing eventually show up as employment.

word.definition: A quick, sharp return or counterstroke, delivered immediately after an opponent's attack has been parried; by extension, a rapid retaliatory action or retort.
word.etymology: From French riposte, borrowed from Italian risposta ('answer'), ultimately from Latin respondere ('to answer'). It entered English in the early 1700s as a fencing term for the counterthrust that follows a parry, and only later widened to argument and, more recently, to armed retaliation — keeping in every sense the requirement that the answer be immediate.
word.example: Iran's riposte to the Larak Island strike came within hours: missiles and drones aimed at the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan, eight of them intercepted.
